full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN, with medium confidence.** The closest match is Fu & Wang (2008). Their model differs from this one in some details, but I don't expect those details to change the qualitative outcome.

**1. Model family.** This is a coevolving or adaptive opinion model, in the voter-model lineage but with a majority-rule update. Nodes take one of G=4 discrete opinions on an Erdős–Rényi graph. Each node adopts its local majority, and a node with a discordant link cuts it and rewires to a random node of the same type. This is homophilic rewiring, also called "rewire-to-same" or "partner switching".

**2. The specific behaviour.** Two things happen together: consensus, and a giant component of about 90% with extra components. Both are documented.

- **Earliest and closest source: Fu & Wang, Phys. Rev. E 78, 016104 (2008).**
  - I could read only the abstract. It combines majority-preference, where individuals adopt the majority opinion among their neighbours, with minority-avoidance, where they break the link to a differing minority node and rewire to a same-opinion node. The rewire target is either a neighbour-of-neighbour or a random node.
  - The network self-organises into connected communities of like-minded individuals, so many opinions coexist. The abstract says diverse opinions disappear into uniform opinion at other parameter values.
  - This is the same two-rule structure and the same consensus-versus-fragmentation trade-off as this system.
- **Earlier foundations.**
  - Holme & Newman, Phys. Rev. E 74, 056108 (2006). They found a continuous phase transition from diverse opinions to most individuals sharing one opinion.
  - Kozma & Barrat, Phys. Rev. E 77, 016102 (2008). Long-term dynamics reach either consensus or a fragmented state in which the network splits into at least two components that are each in internal consensus.
- **Majority-rule updating on adaptive random networks.** Benczik et al., Phys. Rev. E 79, 046104 (2009), is an adaptive random-network opinion model with homophily or heterophily preferences. In finite systems consensus is typical, while in infinite systems a disordered metastable state can persist for a very long time. A later paper says the original adaptive voter model uses the majority-update rule, which refers to Benczik's model. I only saw that second-hand.
- **Review.** Two reviews cover the area.
  - The 2025 review "Opinion dynamics: Statistical physics and beyond" says a majority rule, together with homophilic or heterophilic edge rewiring, leads to metastable states with a diversity of opinions before ultimately reaching consensus. It cites Benczik et al. (2008) and Fu & Wang (2008).
  - The same review notes that the multistate model has "partially fragmented" states where not every component is internally in consensus (Böhme & Gross 2012). That is a plausible reading of the extra components seen here.
  - Gross & Blasius, J. R. Soc. Interface 5, 259 (2008), is the broader adaptive-network review. I saw it only as a reference-list entry and did not read it.

**3. What differs from the literature (KNOWN-VARIANT considerations).**
- **Synchronous majority.** The majority update here is applied to every node on every step (p=1.0). Most of the literature uses asynchronous, single-node or single-edge updates. Synchronous majority on sparse graphs can freeze in small stable domains. I believe this explains why the fingerprint looks unlike textbook consensus: n_components is above 1 while n_giant is about 0.9. I did not find a source that confirms this for exactly this setup.
- **Global rewiring.** Rewiring goes to a uniformly random same-type node. This matches the "rewire-to-same" rule in the standard adaptive voter model.
- **Four opinions.** Multistate adaptive models are documented.
- **Low rewiring rates and ER mean degree 4.** These are parameter regimes, not new mechanisms.

I don't think any of these changes the mechanism. At most, the synchronous update changes the route to consensus and the leftover small components.

**4. Confidence and limits.**
- Fu & Wang and Benczik et al. were seen only as abstracts, snippets or citations, not full text, because both are paywalled. I did not check their exact parameters, so I can't confirm they report the same numbers.
- I did not find a paper that simulates synchronous, every-step majority with probabilistic rewire-to-same on 4 states. If the synchronous frozen-domain effect is the question, that detail is only indirectly covered.
- The model class and the consensus-versus-fragmentation behaviour are well documented, so I put confidence at medium rather than high.
